assessment_summary: The proof contains a clear logical fallacy in the backward direction on lines 0032-0034. The author attempts to argue that because there are only n original vertices in VH, any set of n distinct vertices of G must include all of VH. This is mathematically false, as one can simply select n vertices from the 17 newly added isolated vertices (or a mix of added and original vertices) without including all original vertices. Furthermore, a set of size n cannot include all n original vertices 'and possibly some of the added ones' without exceeding size n. Although the proof later provides a correct justification (that isolated vertices cannot be part of a connected path of length n > 1), the explicit logical deduction made in lines 0032-0034 is fundamentally flawed.
counterexample: Let H = (VH, EH) be a graph with n=2 vertices, VH = {v1, v2}. The constructed graph G has 19 vertices, VG = {v1, v2, u1, ..., u17}. The proof explicitly claims on lines 0032-0034 that 'any set of n distinct vertices of G must include all the original vertices VH (and possibly some of the added ones).' However, we can choose a set of n=2 distinct vertices to be {u1, u2} from the 17 added isolated vertices. This set contains no vertices from VH. Therefore, the logical deduction that any set of n distinct vertices of G must include all of VH is false.
